label: paragraph_title
text: NEW CANTON TAXES.

label: paragraph_title
text: REVENUE TO SETTLE THE BOYCOTT

label: text
text: Powers Told About Procedure.

label: text
text: DOMESTIC LEVY: BUT CUSTOMS CO-OPERATION WANTED.

label: text
text: 〣〣〣〣〣

label: text
text: Further concrete evidence is available as to Canton's intention to terminate the boycott, it being now revealed that the new taxes will be collected unless the Powers intervene.

label: text
text: The Nationalist Government chooses the obvious date of Oct. 11 for the levy to commence.

label: text
text: Reading between the lines it appears that Canton is particularly desirous of working through the Maritime Customs. But should facilities not be forthcoming, the Government will use their own organisation.

label: text
text: The Canton Information Bureau has issued an important communique through Reuter:—

label: text
text: The acting Minister for Foreign Affairs has addressed an identic note to each of the local representatives of the Foreign Powers whose nationals are in trading relation with Liang Kwang provinces.

label: text
text: “I have the honour to communicate to you the following translation of a mandate issued by my Government on October 4:—(1)—The Ministry of Finance is hereby instructed to levy a temporary internal tax on the consumption or the production of such articles as are the subject of trade between the Liang Kwang provinces and the other provinces in China and foreign countries.

label: text
text: (2)—The rate of taxation shall be equivalent to half the usual Maritime or Native Customs tariff (as the case may be) on general articles and to a full tariff on articles of luxury such as silk, silk-stuff, toilet articles, fur and leather articles of decoration, 'gems' and precious stones and similar goods. Cigars, cigarettes, imported wines, kerosine and gasoline, which are the subject of other special taxes, are exempt from this tax. (3)—The Ministry of Finance, for purposes of convenience, may collect such taxes at or near the various Maritime and Native Customs barriers and is instructed to make detailed regulations governing the collection of the said tax.

label: text
text: (4) —Any person selling or buying or otherwise dealing with articles on which the said tax has not been paid shall be liable to a term of imprisonment not exceeding three years and/or a fine equivalent to the times the value of the article or articles which shall also be confiscated.

label: text
text: (5)—This mandate shall come into effect on October 11, 1926.

label: text
text: "It seems desirable to emphasise the fact that the new tax is in principle an internal tax to be distinguished from the imposts levied as Customs duties under the Chinese Maritime Customs system. There is, of course, no intention to interfere with the latter as at present administered, though possible misunderstanding and friction would be avoided if Maritime Customs co-operation should be available in the collection of the new tax by fiscal authorities to be appointed by my Government."

label: paragraph_title
text: Reply to Customs.

label: text
text: That Maritime Customs cooperation is desired is indicated in a letter addressed to the Commissioner of Customs by the Chinese Superintendent of Customs who states:—Further with reference to the collection of the new consumption and production tax, I wish to reply to your specific questions as follows:—

label: text
text: (1)—A tax will be levied based on the Customs Tariff unless for any technical reason such would prove unsatisfactory in which case an effective 2½ per cent. and 5 per cent. will be charged for general articles and luxuries, respectively.

label: text
text:
(2)—The Ministry of Finance would prefer if possible to borrow a room or rooms in the Customs building for the use of a small staff to carry on the collection of the new taxes which would facilitate the work of both the Ministry and Customs administration.
(8)—The tax will come into operation commencing on October 11, 1926, or as near that date as possible.

label: paragraph_title
text: Picket Activities to Cease on

label: text
text: With only a few more days to go, there now seems little doubt that the Canton Government will succeed in calling off the pickets whose activities are expected to cease on Monday at the latest.

label: text
text: Merchants in Canton predict that the restoration of communications will be slow as the majority of the populace will hesitate for a few days at least before openly resuming trade.

label: text
text: Strike pickets at Namtau and Samchun are gradually returning to Canton by railway to-day.

label: text
text: The Strike Executive has appointed Mr. So Shiu-ching (chairman) to receive $50,000 from the Finance Ministry as the first funds to mobilise (or re-organise) the pickets. The Strike Committee is expected to have completely dispersed by three months.

label: text
text: General Chang Kai-shek, in a telegram to General Li Chai-sum (at Canton), inter alia, instructs General Li to complete the strike settlement rapidly.

label: text
text: The Foreign Office intends to publish a history of the Strike movement for circulation abroad and internally.—Wah Tsz Yat Po.

label: paragraph_title
text: SHOT HIS BOLT?

label: paragraph_title
text: Genius of Cantonese Vanguard

label: text
text: FLANK ATTACKS BY ALLIES.

label: text
text: Sun Chuan-fang in a Race

label: text
text: [By Our Special Correspondent.]

label: text
text:
Has General Li Chung-jen (Can-
conese 7th Army) shot his bolt?

label: text
text: After taking Te-an, he marched up the Nanchang-Kiukiang Railway with a comparatively small force and threatened Kiukiang, the headquarters of Sun Chuanfang.

label: text
text: Evidently there has been a race for time. Before other Cantonese detachments —including picked divisions said to be led by Chang Kai-shek in person—could attack Nanchang and start a debacle, the northern allies moved up reinforcements and the genius of the southerners' vanguard has had to retire.

label: text
text: The Kiangsi front has now been considerably shortened. Instead of having columns moving out to menace Hunan, Marshall Sun Chuan-fang brought back several mixed brigades to make a determined stand on this important railway.

label: text
text: Cables from the war zone indicate that the northerners attacked Li Chung-jen from two sides, pressed back his two flanks and caused him to retire a few miles, thus relieving immediate pressure.

label: text
text: It appears that the reinforcements that Sun Chuan-fang withdrew from the Yangtse banks have been sent down the railway to continue the counter-attack.

label: text
text: The northern troops who pushed back Li Chung-jen were brought up from Nanchang and other districts to the south of Tein.

label: text
text: Both sides are now throwing the greater part of their strength into the campaign. It is predicted that a big battle will be fought parallel to the railway—possibly the deciding engagement of the war.

label: text
text: In the south of Kiangsi, the rival armies are content to watch each other. In the north (i.e., along the Yangtse, between Kiujiang and Wuchang) hostilities have decreased considerably and it is understood that General Tang Sang-thee (commanding the 8th Cantonese Army) has come to terms with Sun Chuan-fang.

label: text
text: Colour is lent to this sudden trend of politics by a cable, reported to have been sent by Sun Chuan-fang to the Fengtian Party (in power at Peking) recommending an alliance with Tang Sang-chee (who is to be given the territory he, now holds) against Chang Kai-shek!

label: text
text: Wu Pei-fu is doing very little except, possibly, consolidating his small holding in Honan province.

label: text
text: Fukien is still talking about attacking Swatów but that is about all. Admiral Tu Hsi-kwei (ex-acting Premier) is reported by a Chinese cable to be returning to Amoy to take charge of warships there in a sortie on Swatow.

label: text
text: To-day the prospect is muc brighter for the northern allies.

label: text
text:
The southern coup almost succeeded but the allied counterattack has driven the Cantonese from a dangerous position. Rapidity in getting up to the new front may prove the deciding factor in the next few days.
Control Regained.

label: paragraph_title
text: OUR G.C.H.

label: paragraph_title
text:
Alterations Considered
Uneconomic.

label: paragraph_title
text: MUST BE REBUILT.

label: text
text: Reasons for Choosing Adjacent

label: text
text: Relative to the Government's decision to rebuild the Government Civil Hospital on the lawns adjoining the present site, a "China Mail" representative had an interesting interview yesterday with Dr. J. B. Addison, Principal Civil Medical Officer.

label: text
text: Our representative asked Dr. Addison whether, in view of the expense which would be incurred in erecting a new building, the present building could not be adapted to the changing needs or, in the event of a new building being necessary, was not a site in a more reserved and less noisy neighbourhood preferable?

label: text
text: It appears that the present building is considered by the Public Works Department to have "come to the end of its life" and that, to continue to pay out on alterations, renovations and other maintenance items would in the long run be an uneconomic policy. Similarly, from the medical point of view, it is felt that the only permanent solution to the problem of providing adequate accommodation and facilities is in the erection of a new building.

label: text
text: As regards the vicinity of the Hospital and the question of whether it was a desirable one, Dr. Addison said that undoubtedly it was extremely handy for the poorer classes of Chinese with whom they were very largely concerned. Again, the Hospital was in a far more convenient place as regarded the University for students of which the Hospital provided a valuable training ground.

label: text
text:
By utilising a site in the vicinity for the new Hospital there would be a considerable saving in other ways, it was further pointed out. The enlarged sisters' quarters would still be available as would the present "A" block, which would be re-adapted as servants' quarters, and the present operating and X-ray room which would be the new stewards' quarters.
The site of the present Government Civil Hospital will be used partly as an open space or gardens and partly for providing sites for residences.

label: text
text: The work of building the new Hospital is calculated to take three years. It will have greater accommodation all round, including more European wards; and will be designed to meet the more pressing

label: text
text: needs of the Colony since the present Hospital was erected, some 60 years ago.

label: paragraph_title
text: ARMS BY POST.

label: paragraph_title
text: CONTENTS DESCRIBED AS CANDY.

label: text
text: AN UNKNOWN SENDER:

label: text
text: An application for confiscation of a service revolver and 106 rounds of ammunition was made by Det.-Sergeant Macdonald before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Central Magistracy this morning.

label: text
text: It was stated that two parcels containing the arms arrived from America by post addressed to the Lai Hing Loong firm, of No. 14, Wing Lok Street, the contents being described as candy. The firm took delivery of the parcels from the local Post Office, but on opening one of them found the ammunition inside it. The parcels were immediately taken to the Police Station where the unopened one was found to contain the revolver.

label: text
text: On being questioned by the Magistrate, the manager of the firm said that he was not expecting any parcels and did not know who sent them.

label: text
text: In making an order for the confiscation of the arme, His Worship said that the firm had done the right thing in taking the parcels to the Police Station.
